speechtext: Will the minister indicate to whait articles in the form of processed foods the sales tax is still applicable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Broadly speaking, spices, pickles, relishes, mayonnaise and other specialty articles of the kind.

I wish to ask a question with regard to which I have had some correspondence with the Minister of National

Excise Tax Act
Revenue, who has probably discussed the matter with the Minister of Finance. I ask it for the purpose of clarification so that other concerns in a like position will know what the situation is.
I have been corresponding with a major producer of canned soups in my own riding, who has stated that while the sales tax had been removed from the final product, at the same time the tax had been imposed on ingredients of the final product. I understand that if the final product is produced under a sales tax, a licence number is given to the concern in question, and if that licence number is given, the component parts of the final product are tax free. When, however, the final product is tax free, these components are taxed. The concern I have in mind wished to announce reductions in the prices of certain products in order to pass on the savings to the consumer. This being so, I think the minister should make a statement on the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am familiar with the case which my hon. friend refers to. I am told that the great majority of the ingredients in the soup are exempt from sales tax. The container is of course exempt from sales tax, and the officials inform me that the content of these prepared soups which is subject to sales tax is relatively insignificant in value. I am told that in one way or another, under the licence system, or otherwise, certainly the major portion of the ingredients of these prepared soups is exempt from sales tax, as is the finished product and the container in which the product is put up.

The minister mentioned mayonnaise and other things. Are the artides that are subject to sales tax taxable because of United States content, or because they are considered a luxury item? For what reason are they taxed? It seems strange that any part of a food, even flavouring or spice, should be subject to sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, they are not exempt from the sales tax. They are looked upon as coming within the category of specialty goods or imported goods. A large number are imported; but it is fair to say that with the changes proposed here virtually all, and certainly all the staple food products, some of them even processed or manufactured, as in the case of breakfast foods, are exempt from sales tax.

I notice the list of articles on which the tax has been repealed includes canned vegetables and fruit juices, but the list does not include catsup and vegetable juices. Why should they not be placed in 5849-293
the same category as canned vegetables and fruit juices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Vegetable juices are included.
Vegetable juices are in the same line, immediately under catsup.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a question of punctuation. The exclusions relate to vegetables, canned frozen or dehydrated, but not including pickles, relishes, catsup, sauces, olives and similar goods. Then there is a semicolon; and then come vegetable juices. It may not be entirely clear, but vegetable juices are exempt and the qualification relates to pickles, relishes, catsup, sauces, olives and similar goods.

When the minister was introducing his budget he said, at page 4068 of Hansard, that the exemptions which are the subject matter of the resolution now before the committee would result in a revenue loss for an entire year of about $20,000,000. No one in the house will object to these exemptions; the criticism has been that they do not go far enough. The concern of the public will be, I think, that the reductions in taxes levied in the first instance should be passed on to the consumers just as soon as possible. May I ask the minister if his department or the wartime prices and trade board is interesting itself in that question? There were a good many newspaper articles on that point just after the budget speech. In an article in the Globe and Mail I noticed this:	"Biscuit makers pass on tax cut.
Reduction of two to five cents on a package of biscuits made possible by the elimination of the eight per cent sales tax is being passed on to the consumer." That was an announcement made by the sales manager of McCormick's Limited. I think we all appreciate that it may take a while for some of these reductions in taxes to be translated into reductions in price to the consumer, as inventories move off the shelves. Has the minister any information to give the committee on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That question received a great deal of consideration when thought was being given to the removal of this tax, because naturally we are all interested in seeing that the consumer should get the benefit of the tax relief; that it should not be absorbed in the prices or profit margins of manufacturers or distributors. The information I obtained convinced me the situation was such that in the great majority of these items the reduction would be reflected in the prices. Already it has been reflected in the prices of things like
Excise Tax Act

smoked meats. If hon. members or their wives have been purchasing these commodities they will have noticed a definite reduction. In cases where inventories were low, that reduction would be reflected quite promptly.
The big items in this $20,000,000 saving will be in the field of smoked meats, that is ham and bacon, and in the canned vegetables and fruits. Those are the items in which there is the large revenue loss; and I am informed that the competition feature there is such that the reduction would be reflected in the prices. I have made no purchases myself to. see if that is true, but I have every reason to believe that these savings will be passed on to the consumer.

I am sorry to have to differ from the minister, but out in our part of the country it is definitely conceded that there is practically no difference in price. I do not know about ham and bacon, but on ordinary items it is conceded that removal of the sales tax is making practically no difference, and people have written me to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be that the distributors have not yet got rid of their tax-paid inventory. We made no refunds.

There is also the matter of freight rates. The extra freight must have made some difference, but they say they cannot notice any difference in their family budgets. I think it only fair to report this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be true, but general statements of that kind do not carry a great deal of conviction. The effect on a can of peas or corn or something like that should be two or three cents, and people might not notice it, but it is there just the same.
When you have the head of a great system of chain stores warning the people there will not be any reduction, I am afraid we have to take his word for it.

I should like to ask the minister how a consumer is to determine the amount of the reduction. Is the government taking responsibility for posting schedules or releasing information? If I go into a store to make certain purchases, how can I tell whether or not the entire reduction is being passed on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as I know there is no way in which the individual can tell that, because there is no price control on the particular articles with which we are concerned here. I do not think that could be enforced

now. Therefore we must depend on the ordinary competition between stores. If the tax represented an additional amount of eight or ten cents a pound on ham or bacon, or whatever it may be, the normal forces of supply and demand will operate, I am sure, and the price will represent the cost to the merchant plus his margin of profit. Of course if he has to cut the price below that, he will go out of business. To answer my hon. friend's question directly, there is not, and there cannot be, any policing by the government on the individual grocer to see that he gives his customers the benefit of the lower cost made possible by the removal of the sales tax.
Then this is the list on which these cuts can be expected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. There is a long list, but the main items are the cooked and prepared meats, a wide range of canned fruits and vegetables, and things like biscuits, to which the hon. member for Eglinton has referred1; macaroni, vermicelli, and so forth.

There is quite a difference between the articles the minister has just mentioned. I would like to draw attention to the fact that all canned goods are packed in the summer months. These canned goods are now in the hands of the dealers, not in the -hands of the producers. Consequently in the great majority of cases the government collected the sales tax on these goods quite some time ago. But that is not the question I rose to ask. This paragraph does not seem very clear to me as it is printed. Am I correct in understanding that the sales tax is now repealed on tomato juice and all vegetable juices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I was going to ask the minister if he would mind restating, because I think he has answered the question in part, whether the articles mentioned in the two last lines of section- 1, subsection (a), are excluded from relief because during the war they were manufactured in Canada? I am referring to relishes and sauces, and I have in mind also mustard, which we formerly imported to a large extent from Britain. During the war these commodities were manufactured in Canada. Is the sales tax retained as a protective measure, or what is the reason for excluding these items from the relief which is given to other commodities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not make myself perfectly clear previously. The main consideration was that these are not looked upon as primary foods. They are manufac-

Excise Tax Act
tured articles. They are processed foods, somewhat in the nature of specialty or luxury products. It is proposed to remove the sales tax from all the staple foods, but it is felt that specialty products such as I have indicated contain a high value of processing cost and should remain subject to sales tax.

A moment ago an hon. member asked what happens to the merchant who has acquired these commodities and paid the sales tax on them. He could not very well charge it when he sells the article at retail. Is the tax exigible from the retail and final sale only, or is it exigible on the sale from the manufacturer to the jobber, from the jobber to the retailer, and from the retailer to the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax is imposed, as my hon. friend knows, at the manufacturer's or wholesale level. When the retailer buys his stock of vermicelli or breakfast food, or whatever it is, he buys it with the sales tax included. That represents his cost. No refunds are being made. I made that clear in my 'budget speech. The retailer will have an inventory on which he will have to get his costs, plus, I should hope, a reasonable margin. It is only after he has disposed of that inventory that he will, in fairness to himself, be in a position to pass on to the consumer the benefit derived from the removal of the sales tax. Business being what it is, some retailers may give the benefit right away. In getting a new stock they may average it out and give the benefit at once. In any event they will have a tax^paid inventory on which they can get no refund, and on which they will have to recoup themselves out of the prices of the goods.
It will effect only the current year's crop?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In respect of canned vegetables that is true, so far as they have passed out of the hands of the cannery into trade channels. But we are at a stage in the year when those stocks are approaching their lowest point; therefore, as my hon. friend says, on the new crop it will apply in its entirety.
The minister says that the tax was imposed on the manufacturer and wholesaler. It is only against the one, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said it was at the manufacturing or wholesale level.

Why is there a difference between the manufacturing and the wholesale level? The manufacturing level would represent a lower price, would it not?
5849-293J

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difference between the two is that a licensed wholesaler who buys from a manufacturer can quote his licence number, but the tax is still computed on the manufacturer's price.
I see reference to breakfast cereals and breakfast foods, not including beverages. What beverages could be included? Does it refer to tomato juice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is to exclude such things as Ovaltine or Yi-Tone, if by any stretch of the imagination they could be interpreted as being breakfast foods.
Celery juice is not included.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I pointed out that it is exempt.
Is there any tax on spectacles? Is there a tax on hearing aids? I am not sure about that, but if there is, then there should not be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that there is at the present time.

I notice that the tax is being taken off wheel chairs and complete parts thereof specially designed for the use of invalids. For the life of me I cannot see why people who are wholly or partly incapacitated should be charged for such things as hearing aids. They are expensive enough now. The average price is about $100, and then an additional $8 must be paid for the privilege of having that help, to say nothing of the duty on them when they come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax would be paid at the manufacturer's price.

I do not see why there should be any tax, especially on articles used by people who are incapacitated or who have not the full use of their faculties. Many persons have to wear glasses. Why should they have to pay an excise tax as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have been following my hon. friend's remarks, and I shall give them consideration. I cannot give any undertaking that action will be taken this year, but his observations may bear fruit at some later time.

I notice that the tax on wheel chairs is being taken off; yet they do not cost any more than a hearing aid. Why take the tax off a wheel chair and leave it on a hearing aid? It is only within the last little while that people have realized
Excise Tax Act

they can get relief through the use of hearing aids. We know that there are institutions to help the deaf, and they are doing good work. I suggest that as a gesture of good will, and as an indication that the government is willing to help these people who are doing a fine job, it should take the tax off hearing aids. It has been found that many who have not made a full measure of success in business or in their work have been suffering from loss of hearing. Those people are being rehabilitated, and one is surprised at the progress that is being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall give consideration to the hon. member's remarks.

I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for St. Paul's, and I suggest that the minister should do in connection with hearing aids what he is doing in connection with wheel chairs, including parts and repairs. I have had occasion to go with friends of mine when they were buying parts for hearing aids, and I know that they are delicate and expensive, and the upkeep is fairly heavy. If one is to keep them in operating condition, in the course of a year it will run into a considerable sum of money. As the hon. member for St. Paul's has said, a person who is hard of hearing is under a handicap, and will find it difficult to obtain and to keep certain kinds of employment. This means continuous expenditure for batteries and replaceable parts, which in the beginning are extremely expensive. In my view the cost is out of all proportion to what is put into them. These bits of plastic, wire and batteries add up to about $100-and you can hold one in your hand. Certainly I think there should be no tax, and no duty, because hearing aids involve not only a heavy initial cost, but continuous expenditures for upkeep.

I should like to give my own experience in this connection. I use a hearing aid, although I do not use it all the time. They are expensive to operate. One has to buy batteries, and, while one of the batteries costs only thirty cents, it lasts about two weeks, or possibly not that long if it is used continuously. The other battery costs about $2.50 or $3, and lasts about a month if used all the time. In addition, repairs have to be made. I had mine repaired only recently, and it cost $40. There was sales tax on that. These articles do not last for ever. They have to be adjusted, and they wear out. They are delicate machines. When one considers the disadvantages of lack of proper hearing and what is being done by the institutions which take care of those who are hard of hearing in an effort to make them

economically independent, it is obvious that it is not fair to tax the apparatus which persons who are hard of hearing must buy. To my way of thinking it is no more logical to take the tax off wheel chairs than it is to take it off hearing aids, or spectacles for that matter. I cannot make my representations too strong. Those who are not hard of hearing do not know what it is like and the amount of expense that is involved.

I wish the minister would consider some amendment there. While he is doing that, would he also clarify the situation in connection with special bed equipment for invalids? Are they exempt from the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that they are.

There are special types of hospital beds for invalids which are being purchased by certain fraternal organizations to be furnished t-o people in the community for use in their homes. Is that type of equipment tax free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be exempt from tax when purchased by a hospital. If purchased by a private individual it would be subject to tax the same as anything else.

There are fraternal groups which purchase this type of equipment, not just for their own members but for community work. I am told that these special beds are taxed. Mention has been made of hearing aids, and I would like the minister to do something in this connection. I know of three instances in which extensive distribution is being made of special bed equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have listened with a great deal of interest and sympathy to what has been said, particularly about hearing aids and hospital beds. In considering these I must look at the whole field of equipment used for the care of invalids. That is why I would not want, to give any special undertaking to exempt hearing aids. Wheel chairs happen to be an item in connection with which we have received a number of representations, and strangely enough I do not recall that we have had representations in connection with hearing aids.
You had them two or three years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had forgotten about them, if that is so. I shall have to take a look at the whole field of invalid equipment and supplies. I cannot give any assurance that we shall be able to do it at once. If these items are to be exempt, they should be exempted as a whole and not in bits and pieces.

Excise Tax Act

I want to concur in what has been said by other hon. members with respect to hearing aids. I have had representations made to me in this connection. I hope the minister will not need a hearing aid, that his hearing will be good and that results will follow from the representations that have been made today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope most hon. members of the house will not have to pay the tax even if it stays on.
There are a number of producing wells in my constituency, and I have been asked to find out whether the government would consider reducing the tax on petroleum products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that my hon. friend is referring to the sales tax on petroleum products, which is a large item. While no special consideration is being given to this matter at the moment, I shall take note of my hon. friend's remarks.

I was not present when the budget was introduced. I realize that there will be a loss in revenue from sales tax, and I should like to know what the loss will be in connection with the items covered by paragraphs (a) and (b) of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The estimate I gave in the budget speech was $20,000,000 in connection with exemptions on food products. While the exemptions on the other items will be important to the people who use them, the amount of revenue is quite small. My officials did not attempt to make any specific estimate for the
(b)	portion of the resolution, partly because they did not have too accurate statistics as to sales during the preceding year. The statistics in respect to the food items were more nearly accurate.
We can take it that the loss of revenue for these two items will not run more than $20,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the best estimate we have.

To what extent has the experience of the last few days shown that the withdrawal of the sales tax on these food products has been passed on to the consumer? The total saving to each individual in Canada by the removal of the sales tax will be approximately $1.80 a year and I should like to know to what extent since May 19 the cost of these various items to the consumer has been reduced. Apparently nothing has been done to assure the passing on to the consumer of any reductions of this kind. What are the
obstacles to ensuring that reductions will actually be passed on to the consumer, to the end that the cost of living will be reduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether my hon. friend was in his seat a moment ago when I answered a similar question put by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. First., as to-the reflection in the loss of revenues; as hon. members know, this tax is imposed at the manufacturer's level and the manufacturers or wholesalers make monthly returns. Therefore it is too soon for us to have any accurate idea of what the difference in sales tax remittances will be.
As to the effect on domestic prices, we have no official information, but through the wartime prices and trade board we happen to know that a number of firms passed on the saving immediately. For instance, the morning after the announcement was made Steinberg's reduced their prices on smoked meats and canned goods.
As to how this can be policed, as I said before, under our system it can be policed only by the operation of supply and demand and the forces of competition. The alternative would be a rigid over-all price system with inspectors going into every store to investigate the cost, the mark up, and the margin of profit on any particular item. I think it will be readily appreciated that that is impracticable. The only effective way under our system in which these things can operate is through the forces of competition, by dealers assuring that the price which the consumer pays represents the cost plus a reasonable margin of profit. That is the only assurance we have that this will be passed on to the consumer. It is true of many other taxes, as my hon. friend knows.

Naturally I am in agreement with what the minister says. The minister must 'have made some investigation beforehand; he must have statistics covering the experience of the past showing the extent to which reductions in the sales tax have resulted in a decrease in the cost of living. There have been a number of occasions in the past on which the sales tax has been reduced. My criticism of what he has done in respect to the sales tax is that he has not gone far enough, and has not seen to it that at a time such as this, when the people as a whole are complaining about high prices and the high cost of living-now higher than ever before in the history of this country-any reductions made shall be passed on to the consumer. The government, having regard to the tremendous surplus that it has, should have gone a long way further. I sometimes wonder
Excise Tax Act

whether the members of the government realize the feelings of the people as a whole regarding the high cost of living. I take it that the sales tax was reduced on these items of food to enure to the benefit of the people of the country as a whole, to reduce the cost of living. Is the government conducting the kind of campaign it conducted during the war, to arouse those in business to a realization that the reduction should be passed on?
The prices committee-and I speak of that body with the greatest respect-has been sitting now for three months, and the longer it sits, the higher go prices. What proceedings are being taken against the small minority in business, and I emphasize those words, are taking advantage of present-day conditions to boost prices?
Certainly, if this action on the part of the government is merely a step in the direction of securing in this countiy a reduction of prices, it will not be very favourably received. Talk to the man in the street and you will find that the general attitude is that this is merely a sop, that it is actually meaningless in its results. I ask the minister, is he in a position to say to the committee, on the basis of previous experience where the sales tax has been removed in whole or in part, that, apart from the operations of the law of supply and demand, the saving effected will be passed on to the consumer? I know that my hon. friends to my left talk about ceilings. They say that all you have to do is: Do not touch wages; do not touch the prices of farm products; put a ceiling on prices to the consumer and then everything will be well in this country. When I hear those arguments advanced I think of the fact that in the province of Saskatchewan-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but we are considering the sales tax.

Yes, and I am arguing that it is being reduced because of a desire on the part of the government to see that prices of the things that the people require shall be maintained at a minimum level. The minister asked in the course of his remarks: Are we to police every business in this country? We in this party believe that one of the ways of reducing the prices of the necessities of life is the removal of the sales tax, and I was just mentioning that my hon. friends to my left say that all you have to do is to put a ceiling on prices and then all our difficulties will disappear.
Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend is to be allowed to refer to the election in Saskatchewan the same privilege must be allowed to us all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Lake Centre realizes that whatever leeway he is allowed must be allowed to all members, and I would ask him to confine his remarks to the reduction in the sales tax.

I have found my hon. friends to my left generous in the expression of their viewpoint but equally jealous of the rights of others to place the facts before the committee. However, I do not want to transgress, Mr. Chairman. When we in this party face an issue such as this, my hon. friends ,to the left always rise and say that they wish the opportunity to answer. If you rule, Mr. Chairman, that I cannot point out that in Saskatchewan there is a law on the statute book permitting the control of prices, and that it has not been used by the government of that province, I shall not refer to it.
Possibly the minister will be able to answer in general some of the questions that I have raised, because the Canadian people as a whole are demanding that something be done to stop the ever-increasing cost of living in this country, and if this be one method of doing it I want the assurance from the minister that the saving effected will be passed on to the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that I can deal in other than a general way with the question my hon. friend has puit. Before deciding on the removal of the sales tax on these items, I did make extensive inquiries as to the probable effect it would have on prices. I was particularly concerned with the two big items, smoked meats such as hams and bacons, and canned vegetables and the like, and the inquiries I made led me to believe that the removal of the sales tax would be reflected in lower prices for these articles. That has been borne out by experience in the short time since the tax has been removed.
My hon. friend will understand that in a period of rising prices, unless prices are absolutely stabilized, the removal of a tax of this kind, particularly at the manufacturer's level, cannot be directly related to the price of the article. Under these conditions it is very hard to say whether the full benefit of the tax has or has not been passed on. There is where the competitive forces come into play, as I say. Unless you have a rigid ceiling policy and say that, at the time the tax was taken off, the ceiling on a can of tomatoes was so much a can,

Excise Tax Act
and the tax taken off amounted to ao much, and therefore 'the ceiling is lowered by so much, you have no means of definitely assuring that the benefit has been passed on. However, in the canned goods field particularly I did make pretty extensive inquiries of what the effect would be, and I am satisfied that the benefit will be passed on. I am satisfied particularly, because I have been assured that the competitive position in the field is such that it is bound to happen; but I could not say that you can pinpoint a particular article, say a package of oatmeal, which is included in this list, and say that the full benefit of the tax exemption has been passed on. The information I have been given, and my own inquiry into the matter, satisfied me that by and large that is being done.
The hon. member is quite right when he says that the purpose of taking this tax off was the desire to have the basic staple foods sold at as low a price as possible, and that the tax content should be reduced to a minimum.

I wish to ask the minister to consider for a moment a question that is possibly ancillary to the one that he has been discussing. He has told the committee that there will be no refunds of taxes on goods that are listed in subparagraphs (a) and (b), and I may say that these are items of relatively small cost, and relatively small consumption. But when he is dealing with items of very great cost, and I am thinking in terms of cosmetics, tobacco, malted goods and distilled goods, it seems to me that the department will have to devise some principle other than that which is being applied here, or subject those who manufacture those goods to great losses, and quite possibly to bankruptcy. Take, for 'instance, a carload of wine going across the continent. I do not know whether cosmetics are shipped in carloads, but let us take a carload of tobacco. The time after the goods have left the possession of the vendor and reached the consumer is sometimes a week, or possibly two or three weeks. Cigarettes, for instance, could never be sold over the counter and the tax or duty exacted if it had been diminished in a budget speech; if there is no means provided for protecting the manufacturer or distributor against these huge losses, a disaster may result for those who would be affected by the change. My question is as to whether the minister is willing to give consideration to some principle other than that applied to subparagraphs (a) and (b), which will protect those interested against great losses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am, of course, thoroughly familiar with the grave problem that a reduction in tax on articles of that kind will involve.
I am not sure about this, but I think the principle in the past has been that where the tax is increased the man who has the goods on his shelves gets the benefit of the tax. Where the tax is reduced he has to bear the loss. So far as I am aware, that has been the principle which has been consistently followed with respect to the excise tax on such goods as tobaccos, spirits and so on at the time such taxes were imposed. It arises, of course, not only in connection with these items but on a great many other things such as automobiles and all the other goods on which the excise tax is imposed. I am told that the same principle applies to changes in the customs duty. Where the duty has been increased the man who has a stock on hand gets the benefit of the increased duty, and is expected to take it, and conversely when the duty is lowered he loses the benefit. I will give further consideration to the question which has been raised.

I think that is the answer which is relied upon by some of the departments, but I doubt whether it is a complete or satisfactory answer. As regards customs duty, there may be something to be said for it; but where a certain commodity is liable for the payment of certain taxes, surely the merchant cannot sell the commodity, collect the tax and keep it when he sells the commodity. He collects the tax as agent for the government and must remit it. It would seem to me that the converse does not hold. The tax was on when he shipped the goods, and the consignee getting the goods a week or ten days later is not going to pay the tax because it has been abrogated during the period that the goods were in transit. I do not wish to add to the perplexities of the minister at the present time, but I wish that he would give careful consideration to this aspect of the question because, despite recent bitter experiences, we all live in the hope of a better day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that I am keenly aware of the problem and I will give it further consideration.
The minister mentioned before that beverages were not included, but that certain powdered goods were. Does that include powdered malted milk which is sometimes used for baby food?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Answering offhand, I am inclined to think it would, but I would have to look into the matter.
It is also used for making icing for cakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, that would be taxable.
Excise Tax Act
Why is it called a beverage? To the average person it would be a soft drink.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it is something similar to cocoa, malted milk Ovaltine and Vi-Tone.
Is cocoa covered by this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Cocoa remains subject to tax; so do Ovaltine, Vi-Tone and all these drinks.

In answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre, the minister made a good deal of the free play of competition and its effect upon keeping down prices. I should like to hear him comment on this question. Is it operative to that extent in a market -where the goods are scarce, the public clamouring for them and there is not sufficient supply to go around?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That depends on the goods. There is no shortage of ham, bacon or canned vegetable goods. In my judgment the competitive forces have free and full play on these articles today, and these are the big items here.
My question related to the items where there was not that supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are not many of these items that are not in ample supply in Canada.
The minister is still not answering the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer it directly by saying, yes. The situation in connection with the articles on which the sales tax is being removed is that they are in ample supply in this country.

The other point I want information on is this. The hon. member for Lake Centre suggested to the minister that there should be prosecution of those people who charged a profit which, in the expression I have heard the minister use very often, was more than just and reasonable. I know nothing about this question at all. I should like to ask the minister or the hon. member for Lake Centre if there is in Canada a definite law under which such people can be prosecuted. Is it not perfectly legal to charge 100 per cent or 200 per cent, or whatever the market will bear?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the present time, so long as the wartime prices and trade board order remains in effect, there is a provision that no one shall charge a price beyond that which is just and reasonable. There have been, I understand, investigations in certain cases, and

one or two prosecutions have been started. There was one early in the war in connection with sugar, I think it was, under that particular provision. Lawyers in the house know it may not be too easy to convince a magistrate that a price which has been charged is greater than is just and reasonable, but that is a matter for appreciation by the courts.
What we appear to need is a definition of the term "just and reasonable", in terms of figures, or something mathematical.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is only one way in which that can be done. Someone might declare that a just and reasonable price for so-and-so is the price which was charged in December, 1947, let us say. That was done in 1941. It was decided that a just and reasonable price was the level established in November, 1941, and an over-all ceiling was put on, and also a ceiling on salaries and wages. That was the system during the war. I do not know, however, that anyone could pick out this or that item across the country today and say that a just and reasonable price is so-and-so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the minister and the hon. member for Saskatoon City, I doubt very much whether this discussion is in order. Any discussion must be directly related to the sales tax, and a general discussion on the cost of living cannot be in order at this time.

I need just one line to complete my thought, Mr. Chairman. Lacking omniscience, I suggest that we, might as well quit talking about prosecutions. There is no such thing as prosecutions for high prices anyway.

I did not discuss the budget when it was brought down, and I am trying now to get some information from the minister. If the removal of the sales tax from certain food products was believed to be a method of reducing the cost of living, why was not that principle extended to other necessities such as clothing, shoes, and the like? Why was it restricted to the items in the resolution? I believe that the general feeling is that the budget as introduced by the minister provided for a disappointing reduction in taxation which is totally inadequate to meet the needs of present-day conditions.
As a matter of fact, the reductions such as are made in this section, which, after all, is the only pertinent section in connection with reductions in the excise tax, constitute so infinitesimal a saving to the people, if passed

Excise Tax Act
on to them, as to amount to only $1.80 for every man, women and child in Canada.
I ask the minister this question: What were the reasons that caused him in preparing this budget, to restrict himself to these few items? Why was it, if he was not prepared to go a long way in the removal of the sales tax, that he did not cover other items so material in the cost of living, and in particular such necessities as clothing, which bear this tax, and from which the people as a whole would naturally like to be relieved?
I think the country is entitled to a more complete explanation for the course he has followed than the minister has yet given. He has not explained why, with costs of living constantly mounting, something more along this line of sales tax reduction was not done. Our people find themselves squeezed between a salary level and wage level, which is not rising in proportion to costs, and an increasing cost of living. They find themselves squeezed between taxation, which is very little lower than it was in the days of the war, and a cost of living which is increasing materially from day to day. In the face of this, all that is done to help the average person is the removal of the sales tax on food products.
I submit that the country is entitled to an explanation from the minister, giving in detail the reasons why it would have been economically difficult or impossible to extend these reductions in the sales tax beyond the items actually covered. If designed to ensure some reduction in the cost of living, in the staple products of food; if it was good in that direction, with a surplus as large as there is, would it not have been proper to remove the sales tax entirely from other necessities, and generally reduce it throughout?
I have read the minister's budget speech, and I find there no complete explanation. What was the actuating reason? Why was not this commendable step carried forward so that this government would by its own action contribute a maximum to the reduction in the cost of living as a whole?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend was not here when I delivered my budget speech, but he was good enough to read it, as he says. In that speech I devoted a great deal of time to explaining why I felt that the inflationary pressures in this country were still strong and why I did not think this was a year in which there could be any substantial or general reduction in commodity taxes. In that connection, I said, as reported at page 4067 of Hansard :
In the field of commodity taxes, I have felt it necessary to frame my proposals in the light
of the government's general fiscal program, and am, therefore, not proposing any sweeping or drastic reductions in tax rates. I have considered, however, whether anything might be done by way of a direct contribution toward reducing the cost of living at one of those points where it has been felt most acutely, that is, in the cost of food, and where it would create little additional inflationary pressure.
As I mentioned, in reply to the hon. member for Saskatoon City a moment ago, the articles on which the tax is removed are in relatively good supply and I did not think the removal of the tax would result in an inflationary price movement in respect of these articles. Whether my hon. friend found my reasons convincing, as set out in the budget speech, or whether he did not, I must say there is not much that I can add to them now.
Among other reasons, the food articles were selected because already, by virtue of previous amendments or because of the form in which the original sales tax was imposed, a very large number of food items were exempt from tax; and it seemed to me desirable if I could do anything at all, even if it were rather minor relief, to complete that job and take the remainder of the staple food products out of the sales tax schedule. And may I say that once one takes things out of the sales tax schedule, they do not go back in. Any minister of finance must bear that in mind in deciding whether or not to remove certain articles from the schedules. As was pointed out the other day, building materials were taken out from under the schedules within a week or ten days after V-E day. Now we are moving a step further and have taken out the remainder of the staple foodstuffs, so to that extent we are relieving the pressure on prices.
I cannot give my hon. friend any other reason or explanation. I went into the matter in very considerable detail in my budget speech, as to the economic forces which I considered made it desirable not to effect now any substantial reduction in commodity taxes. If that were done I felt the effect on prices would be adverse rather than favourable, that it would create greater inflationary forces in this country which would push prices up and not hold them down. I concede that these are economic reasons, but they were the reasons behind the budget I presented this year.
Can the minister give the total amount collected in sales tax on clothing last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not that figure here. It is readily available; I can get it and send it to my hon. friend. Perhaps
Excise Tax Act

I should correct that statement; the officials tell me it is not segregated undler that heading.
What is it under?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total sales tax. The total eight per cent sales tax collected last year was $383,012,443; but it is not segregated under the heading of "clothing" and so on.
How is it segregated? Would the minister give the general computation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told there is no segregation.
Has the minister no estimate of the amount of sales tax collected on clothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We could have one prepared, but it would be only an estimate.

No estimate is
available at the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then it can be taken for granted that no direct consideration was given to the removal of the sales tax on clothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that no consideration whatever was given to that question.
The tax still remains on chocolate bars and pop, does it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. We get a lot of money from those.
How much did you get from them last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know about the sales tax, but from the excise tax on candy and confectionery last year we got $16,398,663, and from soft drinks we got $23,767,353, which was up almost $5,000,000 from the year before. That is about $40,000,000 from those two taxes. And it is taken from more than the kids, too,
I may say.

A great deal of that was taken directly from the children, right out of their hands. One of the minister's arguments for not removing the tax from some commodities is that he will not remove the tax from things that are in short supply, but there is an ample supply of chocolate bars and pop. That $23,000,000 certainly does contribute to the high cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Everyone who has a Scotch and soda contributes to that tax.
It is not a tax on luxuries; these things are more than that.

We have one of these so-called pop factories or soft drink establishments in the city from which I come, and I habitually pester the Minister of Finance with letters concerning the removal of the tax on those drinks. As yet I have never heard the minister give the real reason for not taking oS the tax on soft drinks.
He just told us; he gets $20,000,000 from that tax.
If that is the *reason I wish he would say so, because every time I go home I am questioned about this tax, which means a great deal to that little industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps we are getting a little outside the resolutions before the committee. I have discussed the soft drink tax at some length in this house on other occasions, as hon. members will recall, and I do not think we should discuss it now because we are not touching it this year.
Why not take it off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer in a general fashion. The revenues of this country have to be raised; they cannot just be picked out of thin air. Hon. gentlemen want me to spend money on this thing and that thing, and we have to raise the revenues in order to pay the shot. For the time being we are raising them to the extent of more than twenty million dollars by a tax on soda water, Coca-Cola, and so on.
What about the surplus?

I do not know whether the minister will be alble to answer the question I want to ask, but I am interested in the sales tax on petroleum products, because it enters definitely into the cost of production of the people in my constituency. I would ask the minister how much revenue was raised through the sales tax on petroleum products, and if there are any exemptions. Is any industry or any group of industries exempt from the sales tax on petroleum products.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I said to the hon. member for Lake Centre, I do not have any breakdown of the total sales tax revenues from different items. An estimate could be prepared, of course; one could take the volume of sales of the different petroleum products such as gasoline, fuel oil, kerosene and so on, and estimate what the sales tax would be, but the figures with respect to the sales tax revenues are not broken down in such a way that I could give my hon. friend how much

Excise Tax Act
revenue was derived from that product. It would be substantial, of course, because the sale of those products in Canada is substantial.
I could have an estimate made, perhaps, but it would be only an estimate.
Are there any exemptions? Is anyone exempted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed by the officials sitting before me that they know of no case in which an exemption from the sales tax on petroleum products is granted.
For instance, would crude oil used in locomotives be subject to that tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is the minister considering relieving the farmers and primary producers of the sales tax on petroleum products in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, of course every year consideration is given to all these taxes in drawing up the budget plans, but it is extremely difficult to exclude a particular type of consumer from the operation of the sales tax, for reasons I think my hon. friend will appreciate. The sales tax is not a retail tax like the gasoline tax in the provinces, for instance. It is put on at the manufacturer's level, and when he is producing his product and selling it he does not know who will be the ultimate consumer. So the only way to do that would be through some system of refunds.
I should think the better way to approach that subject would be a complete exemption from sales tax, instead of trying to administer it by not making it applicable to a certain class of user. In any event, I am told none of these products is exempted from the sales tax now, and certainly there are no cases where a particular purchaser or user is exempted.
Fuel oil for tractors could be coloured in such a way that it would not be hard to keep separate.

On several occasions it has been stated that the sales tax on building materials was removed shortly after V-E day. Being one of those unfortunate people who are trying to build houses, I can assure the minister that a great many building materials still pay the tax. I notice that here he is including crushed stone or crushed gravel. This is one of the basic, and perhaps the most basic, of all building materials. I should like to ask the minister and his department to give a list of the building materials excluded from the sales tax. I know definitely I had to pay a sales tax on copper pipes, bathtubs and things like that only last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on bath tubs; I do not think so. The crushed stone and crushed gravel items are for use in roads. I am informed they have been exempted when used in building construction. They are exempted under the heading of "building stone". Shower baths, bathtubs, basins, faucets, lavatories, sinks and laundry tubs are exempt from sales tax now.

I received an invoice quite recently where I had to pay in respect of copper sheeting for flashing. That is definitely a building material. If the sales tax is still being collected, may I suggest that serious consideration be given to widening the group of building materials on which sales tax is not to be collected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall take note of my hon. friend's remarks. I have no doubt that flashing of the type he has described would be subject to tax. It is used, of course, for purposes other than building. However, prepared roofings are all exempt from tax. Items of this kind, while they are expensive, are comparatively minor when compared with the total cost of any building. The major items are, and for some time have been exempt from sales tax.
Before we leave the food items, I should like to refer to meats and poultry. Does this mean that all cooked, canned, frozen and smoked or dried meat products are exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
I notice that in connection with fish the words "cooked, frozen, smoked or dried" are not included, and that mention is made only of the canned variety.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were exempt before. The only type of fish which was not was canned fish, and that is now included.

Then there is a matter which I believe the minister forgot when he was making up this item. I suggest that he did not give consideration to the double taxation in connection with raw furs, especially silver foxes. This matter has been considered for several years, and is one of the many unjust taxes. This is the most unjust of all.
A farmer receives, we will say, $60 for a certain type of fox skin. Then it goes to the processing plant to be processed. The processing plant must pay the government $5 on that skin for the privilege of processing it. The actual processing cost may be only $3 or $4. However, if it costs $5, that brings the skin up to $60. Then it goes to the manufacturer, and his cost would be about $25,
Excise Tax Act

bringing the article up to $85. Then a retail mark-up is decided upon, and the article reaches $120. Then the government says, "We must have an eight per cent sales tax on that." This article, which costs originally $50, when it goes into the retail trade is taxed at the rate of about 32i per cent. It seems ridiculous that there should be double taxation, once for processing and again for manufacturing. I believe this eight per cent sales tax on an article of that kind should have the minister's careful consideration.
Would the minister answer my colleague?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood that he was just bringing the matter to my attention. I know there are two taxes. There is the tax of ten per cent imposed on the processor and dyer, and then the eight per cent sales tax on the manufacturer's price to the retailer.

It seems so ridiculous to have a processing tax. I believe the way it originated was that the people who were imposing the tax did not keep in mind that there was a difference between processing and manufacturing. I believe they thought processing was manufacturing. The fact is that processing is the procedure of getting the article ready for manufacture. The manufacturer then prepares the article for the consumer. I believe, if the minister would ask someone in his department to look into the matter, it would receive consideration. Instead of having an eight per cent sales tax, the consumer is paying about 32J per cent, which is really ridiculous.

Why has the minister retained cocoa in the classification which continues to pay the sales tax? Surely it is not a luxury item. It is preferred by many people, and particularly young children, as a beverage to be used in place of tea, coffee, or milk taken alone. Furthermore, I understand that cocoa is the basis for chocolate, and in view of the fact that there is a tax on chocolate bars, and perhaps other forms of chocolate in its manufactured state, there does not seem to be much reason for retaining cocoa in the class which is subject to eight per cent sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Beverages have not been included in the schedule as being exempt. Tea, coffee, cocoa, Postum, Vi-Tone, Ovaltine and these other beverages are still subject to sales tax. We felt that for this year we were not going into the beverage field, so far as that is concerned.
Are tea and coffee subject to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member will
recall that last fail customs duties were lowered on tea and coffee; but they are subject to sales tax.
I would suppose that cocoa would come in first in the form of a bean. It would .be imported in that form, and would not be a beverage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that it is not subject to sales tax when used in the manufacture of chocolate, or these other things.
But it is, when it is bought in a can, for household use.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Cocoa for beverage purposes, put up in a can, is subject to sales tax in the same way as tea or coffee or other prepared drinks..

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
2.	That the excise tax on the price of admission to places of amuseipent be repealed.
Mr. MoLURE: Was this taken off so that the seven provinces which had entered into an agreement with the government in respect of provincial relations might have an opportunity of placing it on? I notice that already several of the provinces have put this tax on at a rate higher than the federal tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was not taken off in order that seven or nine provinces should necessarily have an opportunity of putting it on. It was taken off for this reason, that in April of last year during the course of the discussions with officials of Nova Scotia in particular-but it had come up with the other provinces-it was represented to me that this amusement tax and other taxes-there was the amusement tax and the gasoline tax and one or two others-were taxes which, because of t'heir nature, were appropriate for use by provincial taxing authorities. I wrote to the Premier of Nova Scotia at that time-and the letter was tabled in the house-stating that I recognized that the provinces had a special interest in this type of tax, and that it would be the policy of the dominion government to withdraw from this field as soon as it was practicable to do so. It was in pursuance of that statement of policy that it was decided to withdraw from that field this year. I did venture to express the hope in my budget speech that, wherever it was possible to do so, the provinces would not go into the field and the taxpayers would get the benefit. As far as I know, my own province of Quebec has not done so, but in some of the other provinces .they have.

Excise Tax Act
It was recognized by the government that this was a provincial field of taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it was not. It was not recognized as a field to which the provinces could claim exclusive jurisdiction. If I remember correctly, the language I used was that this tax among others was a tax in which the provinces had a special interest by reason of its nature. For that reason we proposed to withdraw from the field as far as it was practical to do so.

The point I am getting at is that the request came from the premier of one of the provinces that it was a field of taxation which they would like to be in. As a consequence, the request was made by the Premier of Nova Scotia that the federal government should get out of this taxation field; that was done because it was understood that the Premier of Nova Scotia wanted to get into the field himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, and I do not think he has.

What I say is perfectly logical. It has not been done by the federal government with any thought of saving money for the public. In his statement the minister said that he hoped the provinces would not impose the tax again, but this tax was collected by most provinces before the dominion government stepped into the field. I am perfectly certain that when the Premier of Nova Scotia asked the dominion to get out of this taxation field he did so because he wanted to get into that field himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so. This tax was put on during the war and we have now withdrawn it. If there were another war we might have to go into this field again. Whether a province does or does not go into the field again I think would be a matter for the province to determine in the light of its revenue position. If it does not need to impose the tax it should not take it from its citizens.
This was a tax field of the provinces before the war and it was taken over by the dominion by mutual consent when the war came on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I should like to say a few words in regard to the retail purchase tax in so far as it affects the jewelry business. Representations have been made to the minister from time to time by the thousand or more jewelers across this country with a view to the removal of this tax, which was first applied in 1942 as a war measure. I remember well, when it was introduced, that it was stated by the then minister of finance that the reason for its introduction was to divert wartime earnings into war savings. It has been continued since the war, and has had the result of discriminating against those engaged in the jewelry business.
It might be pointed out that if one sets up housekeeping a diningroom can be equipped with furniture that is not subject to tax, whereas the silver dishes and plates on the table are subject to the tax. I do not know whether the minister realizes the degree to which many jewelers generally throughout the country are experiencing a falling off in business since the end of the war. During the days of the war their business incident to the departure of men and women into the armed forces was satisfactory. Of late jewelers in my constituency and throughout the province of Saskatchewan have informed me that their businesses are shrinking in total sales and that one reason is the continuance of the purchase tax. Having regard to the fact that this tax was introduced during the days of war for one purpose, I would ask the minister if the time has not come for the removal of this tax in the interests of one specialized form of business which alone is subject to its effects.
Taxation is necessary, as the minister has pointed out, and must be secured by him in order to meet the cost of government but surely one business in our country should not be singled out for discrimination. If we believe in the maintenance in this country of private business and private enterprise, everything possible should be done to equalize taxation among all classes of business, instead of placing on the shoulders of one group performing and discharging, as do the jewelers, a necessary function and service, a tax more grievous to be borne than that borne by any other business. I ask the minister whether he will not even now give consideration to the removal of this tax which rests so heavily on this one business.

I should like to endorse all the things which the hon. member for Lake Centre has said.

This is a tax which I should like to get rid of just as soon as it is feasible. Has the minister the provincial figures?

No. As I said, I should like to get rid of the tax at the earliest appropriate time, but this is not a year in which I felt the tax could be removed, inflationary pressures being what they are and the volume of public spending being what it is. The figures show that people are still purchasing these articles in pretty substantial volume. The removal of the tax on flatware will, of course, reduce our revenues appreciably. That is the sort of article from which I should be glad to see it removed. I do not know that one can quarrel too much with the twenty-five per cent tax on such goods as costume jewelry and the like at the moment.
The hon. member for Saskatoon City is quite right when he says it is the type of tax that lends itself to evasion by the small dealer who is not too honest. That is one of the reasons why it is the sort of tax that I personally would like to get rid of as soon as I could, but I do not think that in a budget such as I am bringing down this year, a budget in which there is no substantial reduction in taxes, and by which we are trying to counteract inflationary forces and pay off debt, I could go out of the jewelry tax. That is the reason which prompted it. I say frankly it is one of the taxes that was put on during the war, and one which I would like to get rid of just as soon as circumstances will permit.
Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's)1: The removal of the tax would not be inflationary, would it? It would be anti-inflationary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say it would be inflationary. My hon. friend may have his own opinion as to that. He and I differ there.

I should like to say a word about this tax in view of the fact that when I was home at Easter I called at one store in Calgary and at another in Drumheller. I did mention at that time that a presentation would be made to the minister when his estimates were before the house. In the stores in smaller towns where jewelry is sold it is quite a hardship to have a twenty-five per cent tax charged on these items. It will be generally agreed, though, that the reduction on silver-plated articles will do a good deal to relieve the situation; but, generally speaking, the jewelers in the small places are finding it extremely difficult to compete in markets where
Excise Tax Act

other items are available. Particularly do you find that in western Canada.
So far as I could, I have endeavoured to get a comparison between the jewelry business in the east and the west. It is a pretty difficult thing to look at stores and try to estimate where the greater amount of business is done. In my opinion much more business is being done in the city of Ottawa than in the city of Drumheller. I think the reason for that is that Ottawa is what might be called a government city. There is a steady payroll in this city. On the other hand, in the western country most of the trade of the jewelry stores comes from the country areas. This tax imposes a great deal of hardship on the smaller communities, and they have made strong protests against what they call a discriminatory tax. I quite appreciate the minister's view in expressing the opinion that he had to get revenue from somewhere, but some of these businesses are pretty hard pressed. Some of them find it difficult to keep going. If some relief could be given to them I am sure that they would all appreciate it. If the minister would give consideration to it, even in this budget, it would be of great benefit to many business people.

The minister has indicated that this is the kind of tax he would like to get rid of if the time were ripe. I wish to suggest to him in all seriousness that he will never have a better opportunity to get rid of it than now. He does not need it for revenue purposes, and the discrimination which was so abundantly proven last year, has been proven again this year. It has been established that it will continue unless he greatly expands the scope of the present budget proposals. As a matter of fact, his recognition of the problem presented by this discriminatory tax is manifested in the fact that he has brought in this resolution at all. But the resolution is in such restricted terms that very little relief will be given by the proposals. After all, it is confined now simply to plated flatware and to alarm clocks that have a retail selling price of not more than $10. I suggest that the problem which is recognized by the minister, but for which there is no adequate solution in the budget resolution, is one that does call for re-examination of the situation.
It has been pointed out here, as it was pointed out last year in the budget debate, that this luxury tax, as it has been called from the outset, owed its origin to government wartime policy, which was a deliberate policy on the part of the government to siphon off production from this class of commodity into those commodities which more directly assisted the war effort. That entire situation which occasioned the imposition of the tax in the 
first place is gone. The whole basis of the case offered by the government in support of the tax when it was first imposed has gone. We should remember the words used by the Premier of Nova Scotia in a communication to the government on April 21, 1947. Speaking of these taxes, he said:
These taxes, along with a considerable number of other taxes such as those on gasoline, soft drinks, candy bars, luggage, clocks, jewelry, furs and the like, were imposed by the dominion during the war emergency. I imagine that most governments are more anxious to take taxes off than, to put them on.
I commend these words of the Premier of Nova Scotia to the Minister of Finance. I urge upon him that the time has come-some of us think the time has long passed-when this tax ought to be removed in its entirety.
Mention has been made of the discrimination that it creates as against the jewelry trade. That has been abundantly shown. The hon. member for Peterborough West has shown how it operates so unfairly against manufacturers of watches and other forms of jewelry. There is also quite a broad range of articles that perhaps do not lend themselves to classification, directly speaking, as jewelry, but are nevertheless handled through the same outlets as jewelry. The minister has referred to costume jewelry, but there are a great man3r other things to which this tax applies. There are all the leather goods, and luggage of all kinds. If my recollection is correct, luggage bears a thirty-five per cent tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the same tax.

No. I am dealing with the taxes that are imposed upon goods that are handled through the same outlets in many cases. If I remember rightly, the tax on luggage is thirty-five per cent. To that you add the eight per cent sales tax, which makes forty-three per cent right there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is at the manufacturer's level.

Yes, and with the pyramiding that goes on, I am informed by those who are dealing in these goods that it is nearer sixty per cent or seventy per cent by the time it reaches the consumer.
With respect, Mr. Chairman, I should think there is no occasion now to continue taxes of that kind; there is no occasion for such heavy and harsh taxes being continued into peacetime. Pens and pencils are another example. Surely to goodness we are not going to say that fountain pens and pencils are a luxury in 1948 to which a luxury tax of a heavy amount should be applied. These taxes keep on pyramiding and pyramiding.

Excise Tax Act
Then, there are very unfair applications of these taxes. Last year in my remarks on the budget I drew attention, or sought to draw attention, to the way in which this indirect tax was collected from the consumer. In the case of purchases from florists, this is the situation to which I drew attention. If you buy cut flowers in a florist shop today you do not pay the luxury tax, but if you buy flowers in a vase you pay tax, not only on the vase but on the flowers as well.
That has a counterpart in connection with leather goods. A wallet or billfold, if there is a pad of paper included with it, even of cheap quality, can be sold todlay as an article of stationery and does not pay the tax. If the same wallet or billfold did not have the cheap paper pad inside, it would bear the thirty-five per cent luxury tax imposed on leather goods.
This kind of tax has been called discriminatory, and it is so in many respects. It is discriminatory as against the retail vendors who sell goods of this description. It bears heavily upon them, and in that sense they are being singled out for the imposition of the tax. Those who are purchasing this kind of goods are also singled out. Along with that, you have a number of anomalous situations created by the effects of this discriminatory tax.
I suggest to the minister that the way to correct the anomalies is to go to the root of the problem and eliminate the tax. He has expressed his dislike of it, and I think it is fair to say he has expressed disapproval of this kind of tax. I urge him to go the whole way now. He has recognized the problem, and he will never have a better opportunity of eliminating a tax of this kind, which has no legitimate excuse for continued existence. I urge him to go the whole way and cut the tax out.
The minister himself has conceded the possibility of evasion of the tax and I am curious to know what his estimate may be. Do we get half of what we should get, or a quarter, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is anyone's guess. I do not know how many dishonest people or how many dishonest merchants there are in the country. I have proceeded on the assumption that the majority of people are honest and pay their taxes and their bills, and I should think that, in proportion to the amount of tax collected, the loss would be small. But there is no means of forming a particularly accurate estimate. The officials of the department inform me that there have been a considerable number of prosecutions, and that
always has a salutary effect in helping people to maintain their naturally honest instincts. I have no doubt that it is helping in the collection of the tax.
Has the minister considered putting it on the manufacturer's level? The minister would be sure of collecting it; it would ease the burden on the consumer, and he would get as much money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Speaking generally-I do not wish to have the words I say twisted-I prefer a tax of this kind, on the manufacturer's level, to a retail tax, if only to avoid the sort of thing suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon City, that it is obviously harder to collect it from a large number of retailers, and to police it, than where taxes are imposed at the wholesale level. On the other side of the picture, where you impose a sales tax at the wholesale level, it tends to pyramiding a bit, and the retailer takes his margin of profit on cost plus tax. I cannot say that I disapprove this tax, as the hon. member for Eglinton suggests, but it is the type of tax I should like to eliminate at the earliest available opportunity. This budget, however, does not present that opportunity.
Does the United States tourist pay the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes. It is a retail purchase tax.
That is what is hurting Canadian business.

If the

They could take back $400 worth, and anything we could do to encourage them would be all to the good. If this type of goods could be exported through the mails without payment of tax that would be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that can be done. The tourist can purchase an article and have it shipped to his home town and it will be free of tax, but I do not know whether he could avail himself of this tourist exemption of $300 or $400, because my understanding was that he had to take the goods back with him when he returned. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
