I take exception to the loose manner in which the minister and other members speak of pyramiding. It is not fair to the retailers of Canada. They are doing business under conditions that are harder than ever before. They are using closer markups today than in years gone by, -owing to increased prices, and there is no such thing as pyramiding a twenty-five per cent increase. The -buyer goes in and looks at an article. It is sold at SI, $1.50, $2.00, and it is easy to compute the twenty-five per cent. There is no pyramiding of any kind so far as that is concerned. I certainly think it is unfair for so many members, as well as the minister, no doubt unintentionally, to use the word "pyramiding" in a -wrong sense. I think I should say that in fairness to the retailers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My remarks were not intended as a criticism of the retailers, and perhaps the word "pyramiding" was unfortunate. It is proper and necessary for the retailer to add his mark-up or margin of profit -on cost, which includes the tax involved; and I was simply saying that, in the case of a retail tax, the retailer puts the tax right on and the purchaser knows what he is paying, whereas, when it is imposed at the wholesale level, of necessity it is collected by the manufacturer and there must be a percentage mark-up by the retailer; otherwise he could not stay in business.

''Pyramiding" is a proper term to apply to -what happens, and it is not used in criticism of the retailer, the wholesaler or the jobber. They all do the same. It is inherent in that kind of tax. It is no use talking about an eight per cent sales tax as though that were the tax the consumer pays, because in practically all cases it is about doubled by the time the article is sold over the counter to the consumer, since the wholesaler has his mark-up and so have the jobber and the retailer. No criticism of the retailer is intended.
That is a lawyer talking.

Why should he continue for another year a tax on such things as fountain pens, watches, trunks, billfolds and shopping bags as a luxury tax, when oil paintings, oriental rugs and expensive furniture are not and have not been subject to such a tax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 20 last, before moving the adjournment of this debate, during the few moments at my disposal I placed a few remarks on record. May I recall to you that I then brought to the attention of the house the necessity of protecting and maintaining our dairy industry, which has been established and developed in Canada for three centuries in conformity with the geographic and climatic conditions that exist here, as well as the nature of our soil, so that today the production of milk and butter can be increased to an extent beyond the requirements of Canadian consumers. I also urge that the huge amount of money invested in livestock, buildings and equipment for the maintenance of the dairy industry should be taken into serious consideration, and that, as a matter of principle, artificial production should not supersede natural production.
Having this in mind, let me go on to point out that most of the vegetable ingredients used in this new, so-called good and nutritive margarine have to be imported, with the greater part of the oil seeds required being grown in the United States. Soya beans are grown in Canada on only a very small scale, and they are neither the best nor the cheapest source of oil for margarine. In the United States today the chief sources of oil are cottonseed and peanuts, neither of which is produced in Canada. Even if we tried to do so, it is hardly likely we would succeed in cultivating cottonseed and peanuts here. So the greater part of the oil seeds used in the fabrication of oleomargarine cannot be acclimatized to our country. On the other hand, if soya beans or any other oil seeds that are grown here should be used in the manufacture of margarine the result would be a greater shortage of oils for other domestic uses.
Can we forget, Mr. Speaker, that a few weeks ago this house adopted a measure im-

Dairy Industry Act
posing restrictions on a long list of commodities, which until that time we imported from the United States. If we were to abolish the ban on the importation of margarine we would also have to permit the importation of oil seeds, thus directly contravening the intention of a measure adopted by this house for the conservation of our currency.
What would happen in future if margarine should be thrown on the Canadian market? In a short time we would have a surplus of perhaps 100,000,000 pounds of butter for which we would have no market. In the United States, approximately one pound of margarine is consumed for every two pounds of butter. A similar trend in Canada would result in the displacement of over 100,000,000 pounds of butter, with a milk equivalent of two and a half billion pounds. It would then be a disaster not only for the dairy industry but for the economy of the whole nation.
Perhaps one may answer that the surplus should be converted into cheese; but this market would not be unlimited, and then we would have a surplus of cheese unsold and unconsumed. Canada has never been an exporter of butter, except spasmodically, because of her inability, on account of geographic and climatic conditions, to compete against countries with lower production costs. In some other dairy export countries the economy is based upon butter. For Canada the only reliable market for our export surplus of milk products in volume is the United Kingdom market for cheese, where Canada has the top rating and commands the highest price. If, however, surplus milk were provided through the decreased consumption of butter in Canada the result would be a corresponding increase in the production of cheese for export to the United Kingdom; and with larger supplies in prospect from New Zealand and Australia that market would be over-supplied and unable to absorb the additional supplies from Canada. Under such circumstances, the dairy industry in Canada would be demoralized, with the inevitable result that dairy herds would be cut and farm income reduced.
Let us assume, Mr. Speaker, that the present situation is caused by a world shortage of foods, especially grains. One or two good world harvests would bring relief; but to make a revolutionary change in the economy of the dairy industry in the present temporary emergency would have disastrous effects upon that industry and upon the general economy of the country. There are some 500,000 dairy farmers in Canada engaged in an industry contributing over $400 million to the national economy. To depress the standard of living of this large
portion of our population, together with their families and other people engaged in agriculture, could not avoid having far-reaching effects upon their ability to purchase manufactured goods. In the province of Quebec, the dairy industry furnishes thirty-five per cent of the income of the farmers. It is the backbone of our rural economy. Here is a natural process of converting into milk products our yearly crop which otherwise could not be sold or consumed. On our individual farms each member of the family contributes to the production; and milk production is intimately connected with cattle and hog raising, ensuring to the country more and more livestock to meet the needs of our urban population.
Any policy tending to decrease the production of butter will naturally reduce the output of milk, which is a most essential food for the 'health of the nation. If, in some cases, margarine can be substituted for butter, oil cannot replace milk. As to the present situation of oils in Canada, it is as follows:

are not available now; and when the day comes that these raw materials are available, other products, including butter, will also be in full supply. History and logic indicate that butter prices move with those of other commodities, and at that time butter will be available to consumers at a relatively low price.
I take exception to the opinion of those who state that this question is a matter of freedom. The first principle of economic freedom is to protect and maintain the well balanced economy of the country and consequently the farming industry. The physical and economic health of the nation depends on it.
Butter is a superior food and natural product of milk. Margarine is an artificial imitation of butter. Those who advocate the manufacture or importation of margarine should offer this so-called food, as it stands when made with oil without any colour and flavour for the imitation of butter, as shortening and lard are used in food. Shortening is used as shortening. Seed oil should be used as such in cooking. Margarine may be called "butter under false pretences."

The same conditions existed during many years for farm and sea products, which w-ere at such a low price that their owners were obliged to dump a great part of them as a total loss. Nobody complained at that time that the consumers did not give an adequate payment for farm products, and it would then have been of the utmost stupidity to qualify dairy industry as a monopoly. Today, the nature of this industry is the same. Those interested in it are men and women who work with their own hands and toil, from dawn to dusk, to feed our population.
Far from being a monopoly, the dairy industry is the prototype of private and individual enterprise. When butter was sold at twenty-five cents a pound, it was because the dairy industry was obliged to accept the prices fixed by monopolies. But what would be the nature of the margarine industry? Oil seeds would be for the greater part imported when only a small part of them would be grown here by farmers. But the industry would be operated by one or two powerful companies which would be the exclusive manufacturers. They would control the price paid to oilseed growers and the price of margarine. There is a real danger of creating a monopoly.
I wish to say a few words concerning the needs of the consumers. During and since the war, there has been a shortage of many commodities on account of the fact that we are contributing largely to the relief of European countries. Milk products in the form of cheese and concentrated milk are exported. Our allocation of oil and fats is insufficient for the needs of our own people. This is one of the reasons why butter was not available to all consumers during a short period of time. AVhen I object to this bill, my view is not to refuse food to the consumers but to secure for every class of our nation, and particularly workers, butter in sufficient quantity and at a reasonable price, and to supply them with oil and fats in an adequate proportion. If, by the introduction of margarine into Canada, the production of butter be curtailed, then, in the near future, a serious shortage of butter will happen, leaving manufacturers of margarine free to sell their imitation of butter at the price of their choice.
Margarine is indeed a compound of oil and fats, which can be consumed in a form other than butter.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act and to provide, effective with respect to any succession upon the death of a person on or after January 1, 1948:
1.	That the general exemption of estates not over $5,066 be extended to estates not over $50,066.

Would the minister
explain exactly what this means? I have looked into the matter to some extent and I must
Dominion Succession Duty Act

confess that I am a little confused. According to the provisions already in force, this might mean that an estate of $49,999 would pay no succession duties, whereas one of $50,001 might have to pay succession duties of $3,000. I would like the minister to tell the committee whether that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. The exemption of $5,000 now in the act will be extended to $50,000. In view of the point raised by the hon. member, I might say that there will be included in the bill what is technically referred to as a notch provision. By that I mean that in the case of an estate in excess of $50,000, or $50,001, to use the example of my hon. friend, the tax would be limited so that the effect would be not to reduce the value of the estate passing to the beneficiaries below $50,000. I cannot say exactly at what point that would be, what the gross value of the estate would be, but after the tax is imposed in the regular way it would not reduce the net going to the heirs below $50,000. When the bill is brought in it will contain a notch provision of that kind.
Do I understand from the minister that the present section 7(4) will not be applicable as far as estates of $50,000 and those immediately above that amount are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. Section 7(4) to which my hon. friend refers contains the words "five thousand" and the amending bill will substitute the words "fifty thousand".
Will the minister indicate what the loss of revenue will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did that in my budget address. The best we can estimate is that it will amount to $5,000,000 a year and will involve about ninety per cent of the estates.
I am not quite clear yet on this. From what the minister has said, I understand that $50,000 of any estate will be completely exempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. If an estate is $75,000 the tax will ibe assessed in the regular iway, but there will be a notch provision that if an estate is in excess of $50,000 the tax to be levied and paid will not reduce the net amount of the estate passing to the heirs below $50,000. In effect the exemption would not apply to an estate of $75,000, $100,000, $200,000 or whatever you like; in other words, the $50,000 is a starting point, not an exemption.
The effect will be that estates of $50,000 or $53,000 or $54,000 would all yield the same amounts to the beneficiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that offhand, ibut quite possibly that might be the case.

No doubt the minister, like some of the rest of us, 'has had representations made to him with regard to exempting life insurance policies made payable to the receiver general or the crown. We used to have that in Manitoba, and I believe they had it also in some of the other provinces. Provision would be made for the payment of succession duties by the taking out of a life insurance policy made payable to the provincial treasurer. That was practically free of succession duty charges.
I did not know until recently that was not the case under the Dominion Succession Duty Act. I wrote to officers of the department to confirm that there would be no such exemption. Would it not be good business and sound policy for the minister to exempt life insurance policies which were specifically earmarked for the payment of succession duties up to the amount of the succession duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not thoroughly familiar with this procedure, but personally I am very much against it. It would be a splendid thing for the life insurance companies because it would be a good selling point. But, after all, the average life insurance policy represents the building up of a fund by the person who pays the premiums. There is a certain element in it to take care of the mortality risk, but the savings element in a life insurance policy is clearly determined. It is based upon time and the rate of interest. If I pay $200 a year as a premium for a certain number of years I build up a fund 'which, at an assumed rate of interest, will yield me a certain return at the end. I do not see any reason why the man who chooses to build up a fund to take care of succession duties by life insurance should be in any better position than the man who sees fit to build up a fund by depositing money in the savings bank or by buying government bonds. In either case you are allowing him a succession duty-free asset, and I do not think that is justifiable. That is my own personal view. In my own province of Quebec years ago we used to have succession duty-free bonds, which sold at a very low rate of interest. They have not been sold for years now, and I think properly so. With certain reservations, I think the same reasoning applies to a man who builds up a fund in a life insurance policy in order to pay succession duties. I am personally opposed to that type of succession duty-free assets.

Dominion Succession Duty Act

I am not worrying about the life insurance companies making money, but the succession duty rates nowadays is something to worry about, and it is only prudent financing for a person whose estate will have to pay succession duties to make provision for that contingency. I think also it would be sound business for the government to make certain that the funds to pay the succession duty will be readily available. I do not reckon it as an asset if it has to go to the government. Otherwise it seems to me you are depriving people of the means of taking care of this future liability which is hanging over their heads all their lives. I think it is well to make certain that the estate is not called upon to pay a large sum of money when it is extremely inconvenient to pay it, with the widow and family to be taken care of.
I consider it sound business judgment for a person to take out a life insurance policy payable to the receiver general to pay the succession duties, and good business for the government to have them taken care of in that way. I am not advocating this so that the life insurance companies can make money, but for the reasons I have given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This does not deprive anybody of the right of taking out life insurance to pay succession duties any more than it deprives a man of the right to buy victory, bonds to pay succession duties. The man who sees fit to buy life insurance to provide for succession duty liabilities has to take into account what the duties will be. The point which I am making, and which I know cannot be successfully contradicted, is that it is a method of creating a succession duty-free asset out of which to pay the succession duty liability, and in my view that is not justified. I am a great believer in life insurance. It is one of the best means by which professional men like myself can save money, and I carry as much as I can afford, but I do not think any form of asset of that sort should be succession duty-free. There is this privilege, that earnings of life insurance policies are exempt from taxation, and properly so. I can only repeat that I do not think a man should be permitted to set aside money to purchase a life insurance fund which will be exempt from succession duties.
It is not set aside; you are taxed on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are taxed on any savings.

It is not equivalent to setting aside $10,000 in victory bonds. You are gambling with the insurance company. You pay the
insurance company so much a year and gamble that you are going to win, and they gamble that they will gain. You may pay only one premium.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is a good enough lawyer to know that the business of life insurance is not gambling but a business based on averages. If it were gambling, life insurance companies would be out of business next week. I may pay only one premium, but my neighbour may pay twenty. The whole thing is based on mortality tables. I have studied life insurance law in my time and know something about it. A life insurance policy contains a saving element, whether you pay quarterly or annual premiums. It also contains an item for the mortality risk. But it is a form of saving. If you take out an endowment policy and reach the stipulated age the amount you receive represents the amount you have paid in, plus 3-1 interest, or whatever the rate may be, for that period of years. It is just another way of building up a capital fund, and it was never anything else.

Would the minister
enlighten the committee further as to how this will operate in connection with provincial succession duties? There are two aspects of the problem. First there are those provinces which have not a succession duty but simply share in the dominion duty. Then there are provinces which have their own succession duty laws and collect succession duties, but in whose cases the dominion permits an exemption from the dominion succession duty to the extent of one-half, whereas the provincial duty is sometimes .in excess of that. The resolution does not make clear how this will work out in connection with the provinces in these two different classes. Would the minister make a statement on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are simply increasing the exemption limit from $5,000 to $50,000. As I said in my budget speech, the dominion, in effect, is going out of the succession duty field with respect to estates of $50,000 or less. The two provinces which still impose succession duties will continue under their laws to collect succession duties at whatever rates and with whatever exemption limits may exist in those provinces, and the dominion will collect no succession duties in those provinces, because this exemption will apply to every Canadian, no matter in whatever province he may be domiciled. In the case of the other seven provinces there will be no succession duties collected on estates of $50,000 or under.

The last point is, I think, of interest to the committee. Will it mean in
Dominion Succession Duty Act

the case of those seven provinces that the dominion, by abandoning the field of succession duties on estates of $50,000 or under, will thereby reduce to some extent the revenue of those seven provinces from succession duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, they are not collecting
succession duties at all now.
They are not getting any direct benefit from succession duties out of the agreements they have signed with the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have the option of remaining in the succession duty field if they wish to do so, and the dominion in that case would give credit for the provincial duties paid up to fifty per cent. As a matter of fact, none of the seven provinces which have tax agreements with the dominion is collecting succession duties, so that the practical effect of this will be that in those provinces there will be no succession duties collected on an estate of $50,000 or less.
Is this clear, that those seven provinces will not lose any revenue by reason of the dominion's abandonment of the succession duty field up to $50,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: None whatever.

An estate of $60,000 will
pay succession duties at virtually the same rates as today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At exactly the same rates.
But they will pay on the whole $60,000? This is not an exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. It is a starting point, except, of course, for the notch provision I mentioned a moment ago.

I would draw the attention of the minister to a matter that perhaps does not arise directly out of this resolution. It has to do with the gift tax. The rate of the succession duty tax is provided in the act we are now amending. The gift tax, I think, comes under the Income War Tax Act. There is a difference in rate between the succession duty tax and the gift tax. It seems to me that if a person wants, during his lifetime, to dispose of what he owns, he should not have to pay any higher tax on it than if he disposed of it by will, or if he died intestate and it passed in succession to his next of kin or his heirs at law.
What I should like to direct the minister's attention to is that fact. If he will examine the two acts he will find that the rates are different. It seems to me that the Dominion War Tax Act should be so amended as to conform with the Succession Duty Act so far as

rates are concerned. I hope the minister will look into that. By bringing this matter to his attention, I am not suggesting that he should raise the succession duty rates, but I suggest that he bring the gift tax rate down to the succession duty level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to look at that. I imagine there are some differences.
Is there any restriction on the amount of gift one may make to a charity in any particular year? You have to stay within your limitation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the Income War Tax Act, as my hon. friend knows, there is a limitation to gifts which one can make and deduct for income tax purposes. There will be no limit under the Succession Duty Act; there never has been under the succession duty acts of the various provinces. There is now in the succession duty act of the province of Ontario or of Quebec. The result of the proposed amendment here will be to bring our act in line with the laws in the provincial jurisdictions.
There is a limitation on the amount which one can give without being subject to gift tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is in the other act.

Perhaps there are two
things. First of all, you may give away only ten per cent of your income and get a tax deduction; but if you want to give away additional amounts so that it might exceed the statutory limitation under the gift tax provision, is there a tax on the amount that you may give to charity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no gift tax on a gift to charity out of capital.
May I ask the minister a question with regard to the notch clause? It is not quite the same as giving a gift to the crown in excess of $50,000. Does it work as severely as that?

It is much the same as a gift to the crown of the excess.

3.	That for the purpose of the act, shares of companies incorporated in Canada shall be deemed to be situated in Canada.

Will the minister explain the purpose of this resolution? Is it for the purpose of curing some law that has been decided, because we have all had the experience of having a company such as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company with head office in the province of Quebec and also having its stock registered in New York, and there has been a conflict. It has taken us some time to have the matter cleared up. Is that the purpose of this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, that is the purpose of it. All of us lawyers are pretty well acquainted with situs of shares, and how they could be effectively dealt with and so on. Under our tax treaties which we have entered into with the United Kingdom and the United States, it has been established as a rule for situs of shares for succession duties that the situs will be the country in which the corporation is incorporated. Therefore it seemed appropriate that we should incorporate that definition in our law. Of course that would have no effect so far as possible provincial succession duties

Dominion Succession Duty Act
are concerned, but it will make our law conform with the treaties which we have entered into with the principal countries in which there is a foreign holding of shares.
Where do we find that; where does it come in-in our trade treaties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, in these reciprocal tax agreements. W"e have only two at the moment which have been ratified by parliament. We have one with the United Kingdom and another with the United States. Another one is being negotiated with France, and another with New Zealand. I am sorry, it is only an income tax one which has been negotiated with New Zealand. I imagine there are not many foreign holdings in New Zealand. The two we have at the moment are with the United Kingdom and the United States. We are negotiating one with France which I hope will come before the house for confirmation at an early day.

There used to be a great many companies created in Canada which were held entirely by outsiders, non-resident-owned companies and others. Does this section mean that in the case of the beneficial owner of the security in such a company as that which merely has a head office in Canada, has merely a Canadian charter, Canada will collect the succession duty and not the country where the man is domiciled? Does it go that far? It must be important for us, or important to the countries where the beneficial owners have their domicile.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. We collect the tax at the source, and in the case of persons in the countries to which I have referred, they are given a tax credit in their own jurisdiction. It works both ways.

Is this not too much of a good thing for our country? I am surprised that we were allowed to negotiate such a treaty with other countries, because surely Canada is the only country that has a great many of these charters under which people outside the country own all the shares of the company. Or is it pretty well on a reciprocal basis? How did we manage it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say it is not to the disadvantage of Canada. The United States have that as a general ride, apart from treaty provisions with us. We have this effectively dealt with rule, and I am familiar with it, because I had a case in which it was invoked, which went to the privy council, so that I know all the arguments pro and con. I think this is a sensible sort of rule and it is certainly not to the disadvantage of Canada.
How does it work out in respect of a Canadian who may hold shares with a Bahamas company that holds all the securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would tax him on all his assets, wherever he was domiciled. The only practical effect is in connection with Shares of non-residents, persons not resident in Canada, who own shares in Canadian companies. Under the rule laid down, the transfer place could be established in Bermuda or the Bahamas and the shares effectively dealt with there, and Mr. Smith, who lived in Czechoslovakia, could have his shares registered on the Bermuda registry and he would not be subject to succession duty in Canada. Under the proposed amendment that will not apply. If he lives in the United Kingdom or the United States it wil not have a practical effect because, while we will collect the tax at the source, he will get credit for it in the jurisdiction of his domicile.
Suppose a man has shares in a company incorporated in Bermuda. That is where the situs is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in virtue of the legal maxim mobilia sequntur personam. It would be taxable at the domicile of the owner.

Yes.

Dominion Succession Duty Act
Is that due to a treaty of reciprocity between the two countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Reciprocity helps out. If it were not for our treaty with the United States, the Canadian would be taxed there and would get no credit in Canada, because the Americans proceed on the principle that they collect succession duties on the shares of a company incorporated within the United States. Under our treaty with the United States, the United States authorities would collect succession duties at the source, on Standard Oil of New Jersey, but the heirs of the deceased would take credit for it on his tax liability in Canada, and the reverse would be the case.
If the shares were owned by a Canadian but belonged to a Bermuda corporation, who collects the tax there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case a man might be subject to double taxation. This statute would have no bearing on that case at all. In the case of a man who lived in Ottawa and dies domiciled here, owning shares in Bermuda, or in Tanganyika or anywhere else
The shares being situate here.

This proposed section does not affect in any way a person dying domiciled in Canada, because all his assets, no matter whether they are shares of Bermuda companies, or English companies, or French companies, are subject to tax in Canada.
This section, then, is just to catch foreigners who hold shares of Canadian corporations. They will be taxable in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
There is a reciprocal provision, working vice versa, with the United States and Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And within a short time we hope to have one with France.

I wish to raise a point which is not pertinent to the matter we are discussing ; but there is a cause of grievance in Manitoba, and it is true of all the provinces except perhaps Ontario and Quebec. I do not know what can be done about it except for the suggestion I am going to offer, which the minister may not wish to adopt. Take the Canadian 5849-295J
Pacific Railway Company. Many people in the west own Canadian Pacific shares and, when they die, we have to transfer the shares at Montreal, the registry office being there. Before we do so, we have to file succession duty papers in the province of Quebec and pay Quebec succession duties, which is not justified. The man may have lived in Manitoba all his life, never having seen Quebec, and I do not see why his heirs should pay succession duties on his estate because he has shares transferable on the books at the point of registry in Montreal. In fairness to the citizens of other provinces, the dominion should put in the Dominion Companies Act, or in the acts of companies incorporated under a dominion act, a provision to meet this situation. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has a special act; other companies come here for incorporation, and I think it should be provided that they should establish registry offices in the other provinces so that shares can be transferred in the province in which a man dies and in which he has resided. I do not think tribute should be paid to another province from which he received no benefit and in which he had never lived.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The banks do that. The suggestion is an interesting one. I sympathize with the position of those who pay double duties in that way. I have done my best for some time to eliminate that evil, but only with partial success.

speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:
1. That, in addition to other deductions, a deduction from income for the 1948' taxation year of $500 be allowed to an individual who has attained the age of 65 years prior to the end of the year.

I have received many letters as well as resolutions from different organizations and societies asking that people, especially in the low-income brackets, be given a little more relief. I have a communication from the county council of Peterborough asking that the exemption for single persons be raised from $750 to $1,500, and for married persons from $1,500 to $3,000. This year the minister has given no relief whatsoever.
You voted against it.

I did not vote against it. I have always been in favour of giving the fellow with the small income a decent break. They have not had a break this year.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That was our amendment, and you voted against it.

I never voted against anything of the kind. The men and women who are hit hard this year are those in what might be called the white-collar class. They have not had a break at all. Their incomes have remained at the same old level, with no chance of an increase, but the income tax goes on forever. I feel, and I am sure the people across Canada feel, they should be given a break. So I hope the minister will see fit to bring in some sort of amendment to give these people some relief this year, particularly in view of the high cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have received a great many letters myself-
I'll bet you have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: and a good many representations. Again in this regard I did my best in my budget speech to explain why this year I felt it was not desirable or in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole that we should give any further income tax exemption. I reiterate that since the high point of income tax during the war there have been three substantial income tax reductions amounting on the average to fifty-one per cent; and for reasons it is not necessary for me to repeat now I came to the conclusion, and the government came to the conclusion-
Fifty-one per cent of what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Reduction in tax from the beginning of 1941. That is not generally appreciated; the public memory is very short.
I know my income taxes have not been reduced by fifty-one per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But my hon. friend is in a very high bracket, and I am speaking of the average. I do not know that my taxes have been reduced that much, either, and I am not in nearly as high a bracket as my hon. friend. In any event, I indicated why I did not feel this was a year in which we should make any general reduction in income taxes. A substantial reduction was made last year, which it is true in 1947 was effective for only six months, 'but for the current year will be effective for the twelve months, and which on the average was a reduction of some twenty-nine per cent. That reduction was much higher in some of the lower brackets; and even up to such appreciable incomes as $15,000, $18,000 and $20,000 the reduction was as much as twenty per cent last year. But in view of the economic situation existing today, and for reasons I gave in my budget

speech, I felt that this was not a year for further income tax reductions.

The minister said the income tax had been reduced by fifty-one per cent. He must also realize that from 1939 on the income tax went up like a skyrocket; and fifty-one per cent of that very high income tax does not mean very much. Certainly it does not get us back to pre-war levels.
I should like to mention another matter at this time, which was brought to my attention the other day. I do not know whether it should come under this item, but it has to do with income tax and if I do not bring it up now I may not have another chance. This man owns a grocery store. In his return he listed the amount that should be allowed for the food of one kind and another he took out of his store for his own use. Then the inspectors came along and said, "You have taken that out at the wholesale rate. You should have taken it out at the retail rate."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite right.
No, it is not right. I would not doubt but that the minister himself buys at the wholesale rate in some cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Well, other people do. If you buy in a chain store you may pay a different price from that in another store. Many people buy at wholesale, and in a store of this kind they should be allowed to charge the price they paid for the goods. Otherwise it is not fair to the man in the grocery store or meat store or whatever it may be.

This most peculiar kind of social security I think violates all the ordinary tax procedure we have been taught to expect from the Minister of Finance. Income tax is usually calculated on the basis of income, not on the basis of age. This sort of exemption may permit a man to drop into another category, which will let him off and save several hundred dollars, if he happens to be in the right place on the scale. But it does not put a dollar into the pockets of the people who do not have money. Therefore I think it defeats its own purpose. I am sure the minister was thinking of people in terms of social security when he adopted this method, just as he used the excise tax as a kind of rationing to discourage people from buying things which required United States dollars. I think, however, this is a departure and a contradiction in method in the approach to income tax.

Income War Tax Act
Furthermore, as has been said in this house, this proceeds from the wrong end of a person's life. Today money has shrunk to a degree which scares me. When I go into a grocery store, as I do several times a week to buy simple things like milk, bread, eggs and the ordinary things people eat which are not luxuries-
Butter.

Yes, and butter-the value of money seems very small. And look at shoes. The shoes for which you used to pay $9 are now 815, and the shoes for which you paid $4 or $5 are $8 and $9. Shoes are not a luxury in this country. So this sort of thing does not benefit in any way the people who need money most. I believe the whole income tax structure is wrong, because the government has permitted the decontrol of all the things people eat and wear and use, not as luxuries but just in order to exist. If we are to permit prices to go up I believe exemptions should have gone up as well; but not at this end of a person's life, when his children are married and independent and no longer require consideration, and the grandchildren have begun to arrive. So I believe the minister should be severely criticized for this kind of social security legislation. It is to the wrong group; it is at the wrong age, and it does not do a thing for the people who need social security the most, those who are struggling with young children, those who are on old age pensions, those who are living on small annuities, who come within the income tax brackets but who are not paid at that level.

I do not think the minister would want a false impression to go out. He made some reference to a reduction of fifty-one per cent. I do not think he intended the public to understand that the receipts from personal income tax have been reduced by fifty-one per cent, did he?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, of course not. Perhaps I did not put it in this way, but this statement has been made publicly; it was made in my budget speech last year. I said the average income tax rate on the average Canadian is down fifty-one per cent from the peak of 1942. Of course the income of the average Canadian is away up. The aggregate national income this year will be something like 815,000 million or so, I am told, as against something in the order of $6,000 million in 1939. So that, while the take as far as income tax receipts are concerned is higher, what is left in the hands of income tax payers is still greater.

I think it would be interesting to learn just how the minister makes up that figure of fifty-one per cent. It would be comforting to some of us who do not feel quite that way about it to realize that the figures are arithmetically correct. As the hon. member for Stanstead said a moment ago, direct taxes on individual incomes amounted to $813 million in 1943-44; and it is estimated that for this year, with the fifty-one per cent cut, they will amount to practically $660 million. That is a reduction of about eighteen per cent. So I think we should know exactly how the fifty-one per cent, which undoubtedly is a figure arrived at somehow, has been reached. Obviously it did not take into consideration the total taxation on incomes then and now, and say there has been a reduction of fifty-one per cent, because that is not so. The reason the minister gave may be sound, that the total income of the people has gone up during that period. I think we should know exactly how the percentages were taken, so that we can understand what that figure means. Perhaps it will redound to the minister's glory, and perhaps he will be glad to put it on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not care particularly whether or not it redounds to my glory. I am interested in the income tax itself, and I know my own income tax is down appreciably. I cannot tell my hon. friend how the computation was made.
I did not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But it was made by officials of my department, and very carefully too. They took the number of taxpayers in the latest year and worked out what the same number of taxpayers, having the same incomes would have paid in 1942. The same number of taxpayers, with the same incomes would have paid fifty-one per cent less tax in 1948 that they paid in 1942. I approve the fashion in which those computations were made. It is perfectly true that in the higher brackets the reduction no doubt has not been as great as fifty-one per cent. But if my hon. friend will take his income for 1947 and relate it to his income for 1942, and figure his tax on the two rates, he will find that there will be an appreciable percentage reduction in his tax. And, incidentally, the fifty-one per cent excluded the refundable portion of the tax in 1942.
And also excluded the increased cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Whether a person is sixty-five years of age or over is a question of fact; the taxpayer is entitled to the exemption only if he is in fact sixty-five years of age or over. If the income tax inspectors are in doubt as to his bona fides when he claims that he is sixty-five years or over he will have to prove what age he is.
Before a person gets an old age pension, a birth certificate or some proof of age must be supplied. Will everyone have to submit proof of age before he can claim this benefit?
That should be on the record already.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer that offhand. I imagine the administration will work it out in a sensible sort of way. I doubt if they will ask every income taxpayer to send in a birth certificate.

I do not recall any form that I have ever signed in connection with income tax that contained my age. I am sure that some women taxpayers, particularly those in the thirties, would object very much to giving their ages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say just how it will be administered. It will be recalled that during the war people over sixty-five years of age were exempt from paying the refundable portion of the tax and the income 'tax people apparently were able to administer that without serious difficulty.
Do not the ages of most people already appear on the returns because they would be given when deductions were claimed for them as children?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If an individual was a child
at the appropriate time after 1917 that would apply, but some of us were pretty close to being twenty-one years of age at that time and so that record might not exist.

I did not speak on the budget and there are two or three items I should like to bring up. I have not any particular objection to this exemption of $500 for people of sixty-five years and over, but I think it should apply to other classes of people such as have been referred to this evening. When the average man gets to be sixty-five years of age his family generally has reached the stage where they are no longer his responsibility, but the middle-aged man of forty or in the late forties usually has a family at a most expensive stage. It is practically his last chance to make provision for his old age. I feel that the exemptions allowed to them are not nearly adequate; in fact they are not adequate for people of any age. I take strong objection to the fact that the exemptions were not raised this year.
It is not hard for the minister to say that the government have to have the money. If you have to get money from Canadians who are struggling for the bare necessities of life and are getting no more than $2,000 a year, then Canada is not as great as I have always thought it was. There must be some other way. Tax collections have increased largely in the last twelve months. Wages have increased, but that means little because the cost of living has also gone up, and the increased wage hardly offsets the increased cost of living. Then, lo and behold, when next April comes around, or before that if you are working for wages, you have to pay increased income tax on your increased wages, which means that the little bit of extra money the wage earner got to help meet the increased cost of living went in income tax. This question of greater income tax exemptions cannot be dismissed lightly, because the income tax takes the cream off what men and women are earning, and they have no more chance, particularly those of middle age, of saving money for their old age than they have of flying to the moon. Apparently the only way in which a person can make money and keep it nowadays is to buy something on capital account, like a farm; one day you may wake up and find it is worth $10 an acre more than you paid for it, and that capital gain is not taxed by the Minister of Finance.
The minister in his budget speech made a plea for budgeting for a surplus for a rainy day. If it is sound policy for the country to budget for a surplus, which I am not prepared

Income War Tax Act
to dispute tonight, it is equally sound policy for the minister to permit the ordinary common individual in this country to budget for a personal surplus. The minister says he dare not do that because, if he let the people have any money over and above what he takes from them, they would waste it, spend it in such a way as to put more pressure on scarce articles. I say to the minister, and he knows it just as well as I, there should be greater income tax exemptions for the people for whom I am pleading, because they are not the class of people who, if given increased1 exemption, will be buying goods in the luxury class, or scarce goods, or spending their money in such a way as to contribute to inflation. No, that type of person today is scraping night and day trying to get enough money, not to put pressure on scarce commodities, not to increase inflation, but to get enough to eat and wear for his wife and children and himself. If the minister answers that increased exemptions for this class must result in modifications for those in the higher income tax brackets, that is his worry. I maintain that the man who does not get more than $2,000 a year should not pay a nickel of income tax.
So far as those sixty-five years of age are concerned, I do not object particularly to the exemption that is being provided for them, but I say a substantial proportion of them are in no more need of additional exemption than the young people who are coming along with young families and are faced with high rentals and the high cost of living today. Many of these young people are worried to death to know how to make ends meet, and it is like tossing a wet rag in their face to suggest that if they get $2,000 income tax free they would waste it or contribute to inflation. It would mean an additional few dollars in their pockets to help them in the purchase of the necessities of life, food, clothing and shelter and, in spite of the determined stand which the minister has taken, I think he should consult with his colleagues and work out some system whereby men and women in this country, particularly those in the low-income brackets, will be granted an additional exemption. I know what I have said is not being said for the first time, but I have always taken this position, and no doubt the minister has heard it until he is sick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Year after year.

But I believe it is of sufficient importance that, until the minister acts upon it, we should continue to drum it into his ears. So far as I am concerned, I owe it as a duty not only to myself as a member
of the house but to the people I represent, and before whom I have time and again advocated the principle of increased income tax exemtpions, to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and the committee, because I believe it is an urgent necessity in the economic life of our country today, particularly in western Canada, which I know best. I am making this plea tonight with the minister, because I believe it is my duty to do so and to place my views on record.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before we proceed, may I draw the attention of members to the fact that we are considering clause 1 of this resolution, which deals with an additional exemption of $500 to those who have attained the age of sixty-five years. This clause does not permit a general discussion of income tax or of exemptions generally. That was permissible in the budget debate, but I do not think it is permissible now.

I should like to give the minister some advice on how to draw his budget next year to give the greatest assistance to people of sixty-five years of age, whom I think he sincerely desires to help. I think the minister had in mind that when you are sixty-five, old age seldom comes alone, but people of that age are often ill and need surgery or special treatment for the ailments that come with advancing years. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre so clearly illustrated in his table, the great majority of the people who are sixty-five years of age and over have no security, either for medical benefits or for earnings or for meeting living costs.
I would suggest to the minister that next year he make provision in his budget for universal health insurance for all the Canadian people, and then we shall know that these people do have health security. I would also urge that he bring in at sixty-five years of age universal superannuation, so that we shall put a floor under income as New Zealand has done, and that he use the ordinary tax structure which applies to everyone to recover excess income. We already do this with the family allowance. Regardless of the income of the members of this house, the family allowance is paid out to everyone and any excess income is recovered through the ordinary tax procedure. If we did that, we would know that the people who had the greatest need, those of sixty-five years of age, would be covered in their medical needs, in their food needs, and in their housing needs, that they had shoes and clothing, and that the ordinary decencies and comforts of life were
Income War Tax Act

not beyond the reach of the pioneers who, in their earlier years, had helped to build up this great nation.
We know that the national income is up; we know that in terms of the value of the gross national product it is sometimes misleading, but when you look at it on a unit basis it is still pretty good. There is no one in this house who has not tremendous faith in Canada as a great and growing nation. If we use this other approach, and put a floor under income to take care of the medical needs of this group who need it far worse than the younger people, and see that we would not have poverty, privation and despair in the hearts of people sixty-five years of age and over, and then use the ordinary income tax mechanism to recover excess income, we would have gone a long way toward establishing a tax structure of which we could be proud.

One observation made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre deserves some comment. In his attack on this budget proposal, he did not content himself simply with his argument that it was unfair to apply this to persons of the age of sixty-five years and over. He went on to attack the idea of the increase in exemption, because the people who were going to draw most benefit from such an increase in exemption would be those who had more income than those just over the present exemption.
In attacking the proposal on that basis, he has attacked the whole idea of increases in exemption at their very foundation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not at all; I asked for it for all ages-right across the board.

The whole point of the table put on the record by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was that the people who had a somewhat higher income derived very much more benefit from the increase in exemption than those who had just a very little over the amount of exemption. That argument, if it is sound, applies to every increase in exemption, regardless of amount, regardless of the nature of it, and regardless of the people who receive it. What the hon. member has just succeeded in doing is levelling an attack, as far as his conception of logic would carry him, against the very idea espoused by his party in its amendment to the main budget resolution. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that in the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on May 21, which will be found at page 4255 of Hansard, the budget was attacked, and properly attacked, on this among other bases, first, that the minister had failed to increase the amount of

exemption for income tax purposes from the present level to $1,250 for single persons and $2,500 for married persons.
Did you vote for it?
I certainly said that I advocated increased exemptions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I voted for it; you voted
against it.

The hon. member says that he voted for it; but tonight he has made a direct attack on the idea of increased exemptions which certain members of this house have proposed for a long time.
It is too much to expect consistency from hon. members of the C.C.F. party. Perhaps it is too much to expect them to see the same problem on June 1 in the same light as that in which they appeared to see it on May 21. The fact remains that if there is soundness in the argument that the exemption should be increased-I for one say there is-then undoubtedly an increase in exemption will have the very effect that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre deplored in his remarks tonight.
My quarrel with the present resolution is not on that basis at all. I say certainly the exemption should be increased for those who will be benefited by the increase here proposed. My quarrel with the proposal is that it does not go far enough and include others. It would be a vastly improved budget proposal if the minister would change the word "sixty-five" in the last line to "fifteen." If he did that he would greatly help those who badly need assistance in the way of increased exemption at the present time, the people referred to by my colleague, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, the married people, the people with families, the people on whom the brunt of the cost of living is being cast so heavily at the present time. They badly need increased exemptions.
In his resolution the minister has not done anything wrong. The only trouble is that he has stopped so far short of a desirable objective. There can be no quarrel with this resolution as far as it goes. The quarrel that the committee would like to have with it, if it were free to speak its mind in all quarters, is that it does not go nearly far enough.

In order to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I want to suggest a method by which the minister might avoid in future giving a special exemption to people over sixty-five; that would be by giving a satisfactory exemption to people in the lower income groups at a lower age now. I support

Income War Tax Act
the proposals put forward by other hon. members in that respect. I am not one to rise in my place and demand social services, and things of that type, and at the same time suggest that we can get those services without paying for them. I know we have to be taxed, and that we have to pay for social services in this country. But I suggest that we have to put our taxation on a more equitable basis if it is to be fair at this time to all concerned.
Just briefly, Mr. Chairman, take business in this country at this time. Its profits were never higher. Professional men in this country are doing very well, but most of the working people are just making a living. When it comes to business, it is allowed to charge costs and depreciation. Anybody who knows anything about manufacturing establishments knows there is a great amount of capital investment put into business. That is charged up to maintenance and costs. Professional men have their costs and certain allowances. The principle we work upon is that business is allowed its costs before its profits are shown; and then depreciation and all that goes with it; but when it comes to the human machine, we do not even allow the worker enough exemption to pay for the costs of running the human machine or reproducing the human machine. I suggest that our system of taxation would be much more equitable, particularly at this time, if the government commenced to raise the exemptions so that at least the working people of this country would get an exemption large enough to pay for the cost of running the human machine and maintaining it properly.

I do not want to keep the committee long on this matter, but I do want to say a word about it. I want it to be cleai'ly understood that I am not objecting to the resolution as it stands in so far as it relates to the age limit of sixty-five years and allowing those in that particular class to have a further $500 tax exemption, but I cannot quite see the logic of the minister's remarks. It seems to me that a married man who is. earning a maximum of only $1,500 and who has a family to keep, young children to send to school, to clothe, to feed and to shelter, is just as deserving of an increase in his tax exemption as a person sixty-five years of age or over. I would think it would be much more commendable if the minister had seen fit, provided that he did not have the revenue, to continue the tax on horse-racing and betting, in other words, gambling, or night-club entertainment. I think it would have been much more preferable to retain the gambling tax and the night-club tax. If he had done that,
perhaps he would have had sufficient revenue to increase the exemption, not only of those of sixty-five years but also of all people, raising the tax exemption to $2,000. I think the minister's conscience must bother him a little bit in that regard. I would suggest to him that he sleep on this tonight, and if he can come back here tomorrow and tell us that he has not had any bad dreams I will support him, but I am sure he will not be able to do that. If he sleeps on this tonight I think he will soften up a little bit and give an increased tax exemption to all married people up to $2,000, and to single people as well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the strongest argument for the picayunish nature of this concession was given by the minister himself when 'he indicated in reply to my question that it would benefit to a greater or lesser extent only some 80,000 to
100,000	persons. As has already been pointed out, there are 800,000 or 900,000, perhaps
1,000,000 Canadians sixty-five years of age and over. In other words, this benefit will go to only one in ten Canadians of sixty-five years of age and over, and it goes to the one in the ten needing it the least, not to the nine who need it, as has already been made clear from the table I have given to the committee.
The second thing I wish ito say is this. I do not think the minister took as seriously as he might the question asked by my deskmate, the hon. member for Mackenzie with reference to proof of age; or perhaps I should say I hope that, after he has had some experience in this and has found that one can be sensible and reasonable about it, he will pass on the benefit of his experience to his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
There are under this provision people who will benefit this year to the extent of $100 and $250 in some cases, and $250 is more than the old age pension was when it was first put on the statute books; yet, in order to get that original pension of $240, or the present $360, the applicant has to give definite proof of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why does my hon. friend not raise this question on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Because I am talking about the minister's treatment of the question asked by my colleague. The minister seemed to think there was nothing in it. I submit that if such stringent regulations are made for those who secure a benefit of $240 or $360 in another department, so far as proof of age is concerned, then the minister should either make the regulations the same as his col-
Income War Tax Act

league's or get his colleague to follow suit to him.
The other thing I want to do is to make a brief comment on the interesting remarks made by the hon. member for Eglinton. Apparently the hon. gentleman let the cat out of the bag as to why he and his hon. friends argue so much for increased tax exemptions. Apparently they are aware all the time that if you simply raise the exemption level, without making any other change, the greatest benefit goes to those in the upper brackets. Apparently that is what they wanted all the time. My hon. friend the member for Eglinton did not vote for it when he had a chance a few days ago.
It was covered with a lot of socialistic nonsense.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That same socialism seems to have fared pretty well in Yale yesterday.
We have heard that several times.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglinton tried to make out that there was something inconsistent between my voting for our amendment which asked for an increase in the exemption level, something inconsistent between my supporting my leader in that request, and the table I put on the record tonight. Apparently he did not listen to the speech made by my leader, or he has not read it, because on page 4252 of Hansard my leader made it clear that, along with raising the exemption levels, he felt and we felt that the rates of taxation on corporations, and on personal incomes at the higher levels, should be retained at their present figures. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made it clear-
He said he would keep the present rates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He would maintain the present rates in the various upper brackets so as to make it possible-that is the only way in which it can be done-
You cannot have it both ways.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is the answer to my hon. friend. You cannot use the money that he would use to save income taxes in the upper brackets and use the same money for the benefits he advocates for those in the lower brackets. My leader made it clear that, in order to provide exemption in the lower brackets, which we were asking for, it would be necessary to retain the rates in the upper levels,
bracket by bracket, and that is the point the present Minister of Finance and other ministers of finance have made from time to time, that you have to consider the effect of raising the exemption level on the upper brackets, as well as on those you take out of taxation altogether. My leader made it clear that we want the rates retained in the upper levels, to make it possible to give a worthwhile benefit to those in the lower levels. Perhaps that is why my hon. friends did not see fit to support our amendment.

Many of us did not take advantage of the main budget debate to say some of the things we wanted to say; and lest anybody, particularly the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue, should feel that I am satisfied with the income tax exemption, I wish to make it plain that I am not satisfied. I am satisfied of course, to some extent, with the increase for those over sixty-five years of age. But, like the hon. member for Bow River, I feel that the exemption should be increased materially. By that method we shall increase the production of the country to a great extent and reap benefits that will far exceed those which are being reaped today under the excessive income tax levels and under present exemptions. I see that you wish to call it eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman. When this discussion comes up again I shall have more to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps we can pass this section.
